sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Common web application architectures
Microsoft Learn: Developing ASP.NET Core MVC apps - Structuring the application

claims.text: Microsoft documents N-tier applications as logical layers with specific responsibilities and managed dependency directions. The candidate correctly treats layering as responsibility/dependency control rather than a fixed number of folders or tiers.

Microsoft documents the traditional UI-to-BLL-to-DAL compile-time dependency, notes the testing cost of business logic depending on data-access implementation details, and describes dependency inversion/Clean Architecture as moving infrastructure dependencies outward from the application core. The candidate states this as a conditional design choice rather than a universal mandate.

Microsoft architecture guidance separates logical layering from physical deployment and discusses architecture-style tradeoffs. The candidate correctly distinguishes layering from microservices, names mapping/call/abstraction overhead, and says simple stable systems should not add layers that provide no independent change or test boundary.

findings: Both duplicate source rows are concept questions with the same canonical boundary; the stale generated scenario context was repaired to concept.
The candidate directly explains why layering controls complexity through responsibility ownership and dependency boundaries without claiming a fixed layer count.
Traditional N-tier dependencies, dependency inversion, testability, and infrastructure boundaries are consistent with current Microsoft architecture documentation.
The answer states costs and inapplicable boundaries and does not conflate layering with microservices or claim Clean Architecture is mandatory.
